To take the recursion into account, let $T(N,\epsilon)$ denote the running time of this algorithm (observing that the sizes of $A$ and $B$ do not chance in recursive calls). Then:

$$ \displaystyle T(N,\epsilon) \displaystyle\leq T(\tfrac{N}{r},\tfrac{\epsilon}{16})+\widetilde{O}((r\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}), \displaystyle T(N,\epsilon) \displaystyle\leq\widetilde{O}(\log_{r}(N)\cdot r\cdot 16^{\log_{r}(N)}\cdot(\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) \displaystyle\leq O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) $$

by setting $r=2^{\sqrt{\log N}}$ . ∎

An application of Theorem 1.9 is approximately counting 4SUM solutions. In particular, we can efficiently approximate the additive energy of a set, which will be useful later for the derandomized algorithmic BSG theorem.

#### Lemma 3.3 (Deterministic approximate 4SUM counting).

Given multisets $A,B,C,D\subseteq[N]$ of size at most $N$ , we can deterministically approximate $|\{(a,b,c,d)\in A\times B\times C\times D:a+b=c+d\}|$ up to additive error $\epsilon(|A|+|C|)|B||D|$ in $O\big(\big(\epsilon^{-1}(|A|+|C|)+|B|+|D|\big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\big)$ time.

#### Corollary 3.4.

Given a set $A\subseteq[N]$ , we can deterministically approximate its additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)$ up to additive error $\epsilon|A|^{3}$ in $O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|N^{o(1)})$ time.

#### Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Using Theorem 1.9 we can compute an $O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N)$ -sparse nonnegative vector $f$ such that $\|f-1_{A}\star 1_{B}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B|$ in $O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)N^{o(1)})$ time, and an $O(\epsilon^{-1}|C|\log^{2}N)$ -sparse nonnegative vector $g$ such that $\|g-1_{C}\star 1_{D}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|D|$ in $O((\epsilon^{-1}|C|+|D|)N^{o(1)})$ time. Then we return $\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]$ as our approximation, which has additive error

$$ \displaystyle\Big\lvert\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\Big\lvert\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]\Big\rvert}_{=:e_{1}}+\underbrace{\Big\lvert\sum_{i}f[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]\Big\rvert}_{=:e_{2}}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle e_{1} \displaystyle=\Big\lvert\sum_{i}\big((1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]-f[i]\big)\cdot(1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\|1_{A}\star 1_{B}-f\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{i}(1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i] \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|B|\cdot|C||D|, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle e_{2} \displaystyle=\Big\lvert\sum_{i}f[i]\cdot\big((1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-g[i]\big)\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\|1_{C}\star 1_{D}-g\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{i}f[i] \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\sum_{i:f[i]\neq 0}\Big(\big\lvert f[i]-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\big\rvert+(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\Big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\big(\|f\|_{0}\cdot\|f-1_{A}\star 1_{B}\|_{\infty}+\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\big(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N\cdot\epsilon|B|+|A||B|\big) \displaystyle\leq O(\epsilon|A||B||D|\log^{2}N). $$

So the total error is at most $e_{1}+e_{2}=O(\epsilon|B||D|(|A|+|C|)\log^{2}N)$ . The error can be reduced to $\epsilon|B||D|(|A|+|C|)$ after decreasing $\epsilon$ by only an $O(\log^{2}N)$ factor. The total time complexity is still $O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)N^{o(1)})+O((\epsilon^{-1}|C|+|D|)N^{o(1)})$ as claimed. ∎

## 4 Tool II: Deterministic 3SUM Counting for Small Doubling Sets

The goal of this section is to prove the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Given sets $A,B,C,S\subset[N]$ , we can deterministically compute

- 1. $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ , and

- 2. $(1_{C}\star 1_{-B})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ ,

in time complexity

$$ O\Big(\frac{|A+S|\sqrt{|B||C|}}{\sqrt{|S|}}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)+\big(|A+S|+|C|\big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big). $$

If randomization is allowed, then the $N^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ .

Randomized versions of similar results were given by Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [ABF23], and Jin and Xu [JX23]. To deterministically implement the approaches of [ABF23, JX23], we follow the derandomization strategy of [CL15, FKP24] and work modulo some $M$ . For our purposes, we pick $M\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ such that $S$ has many distinct remainders modulo $M$ , as stated below.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Given set $S\subseteq[N]$ , we can deterministically find an integer $M\in\big[|S|/2,|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\big]$ in $|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}$ time such that the set $S\bmod M=\{\hat{s}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}:\exists s\in S,s\bmod M=\hat{s}\}$ has size $|S\bmod M|\geq 0.9|S|$ .

#### Proof.

We use the same technique as [CL15]. Let $P$ be a parameter to be determined. We will iteratively pick primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\in[P,2P]$ and let the final modulus be $M=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k}$ . At iteration $i$ $(i\geq 1)$ , the primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{i-1}$ are already fixed, and we pick prime $p_{i}$ to minimize

$$ h(S,p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}):=\sum_{x,y\in S,x\neq y}[x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}}], $$

i.e., the number of collision pairs in $S$ modulo $p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}$ . This can be done by enumerating all primes in $[P,2P]$ , and computing $\sum_{x,y\in S}[x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}}]$ in $\widetilde{O}(|S|)$ time by bucketing the elements of $S$ modulo $p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}$ and summing up the bucket sizes squared. We terminate and return $M=p_{1}\cdots p_{i}$ once the number of collision pairs $h(S,M)\leq 0.1|S|$ , in which case we must have $|S\bmod M|\geq|S|-h(S,M)\geq 0.9|S|$ and $M\geq\frac{|S|^{2}}{h(S,M)+|S|}>|S|/2$ as desired. The total time complexity is $\widetilde{O}(kP|S|)$ where $k$ is the number of iterations before termination, and $M\leq(2P)^{k}$ . We now bound $k$ .

Consider any pair of $x,y\in S,x\neq y$ where $x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i-1}}$ . By the prime number theorem, over a random prime $p_{i}\in[P,2P]$ , the probability that $x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i-1}p_{i}}$ holds is at most $O(\frac{\log_{P}N}{P/\log P})=O(\frac{\log N}{P})$ . Hence $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p_{i}\in[P,2P]}[h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i})]\leq\frac{c\log N}{P}h(S,p_{1},\cdots,p_{i-1})$ by linearity of expectation (for some absolute constant $c>0$ ). By averaging, the minimizing $p_{i}\in[P,2P]$ that we choose satisfies $h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i})\leq\frac{c\log N}{P}h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})$ . Since $h(S,1)=|S|(|S|-1)$ , and the second to last iteration has $h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{k-1})>0.1|S|$ , we have

$$ k\leq 1+\frac{\log\frac{|S|(|S|-1)}{0.1|S|}}{\log\frac{P}{c\log N}}<1+\frac{\log(10|S|)}{\log\frac{P}{c\log N}}, $$

and hence

$$ M\leq(2P)^{k}<2P\cdot(10|S|)^{\log(2P)/\log(\frac{P}{c\log N})}=2P\cdot(10|S|)^{1+\frac{\log(2c\log N)}{\log(P/(c\log N))}}. $$

By choosing $P$ such that $\log P=\Theta(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})$ , we have $M\leq|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ , and the time complexity is $\widetilde{O}(kP|S|)\leq|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ . ∎

The following lemma finds an efficient covering of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ using shifted copies of a set.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Given a set $\hat{S}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , we can deterministically find a set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time such that $\hat{S}+\Delta=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and $|\Delta|\leq(2M\ln M)/|\hat{S}|$ .

#### Proof.

Let $S_{0}=\hat{S},\Delta_{0}=\{0\}$ . Repeat the following for $i=0,1,2,\dots$ , until $S_{i}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ :

- • Find $\delta_{i+1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ such that $|S_{i}\cup(\delta_{i+1}+S_{i})|$ is maximized.

- • Let $S_{i+1}:=S_{i}\cup(\delta_{i+1}+S_{i})$ and $\Delta_{i+1}:=\Delta_{i}+\{0,\delta_{i+1}\}$ .

By induction, $S_{i}=\hat{S}+\Delta_{i}$ for all $i$ . When the procedure terminates with $S_{d}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ at iteration $i=d$ , we return $\Delta_{d}=\{0,\delta_{1}\}+\dots+\{0,\delta_{d}\}$ .

We first explain how to implement each iteration in $O(M\log M)$ time. Given $S_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , we use FFT to compute the cyclic convolution $f=1_{S_{i}}\star_{M}1_{-S_{i}}$ in $O(M\log M)$ time, where $f[\delta]=|(S_{i}+\delta)\cap S_{i}|$ for all $\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , and we pick $\delta_{i+1}=\delta$ that minimizes $f[\delta]$ and hence maximizes $|S_{i}\cup(\delta+S_{i})|=2|S_{i}|-f[\delta]$ . Then, computing $S_{i+1},\Delta_{i+1}$ takes $O(M)$ time.

Now we analyze the number of iterations $d$ . Let $\sigma_{i}=\frac{M-|S_{i}|}{M}$ be the fraction of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ not covered by $S_{i}$ . Observe that

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}\big\lvert\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus\big(S_{i}\cup(\delta+S_{i})\big)\big\rvert=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus S_{i}}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}[x\notin(\delta+S_{i})]=|\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus S_{i}|\cdot\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}M, $$

so $\sigma_{i+1}\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}$ by averaging. Since $S_{d-1}\neq\mathbb{Z}_{M},\sigma_{d-1}\geq\frac{1}{M}$ . Hence, the number of iterations is

$$ d\leq 1+\log_{2}\frac{\ln(1/\sigma_{d-1})}{\ln(1/\sigma_{0})}\leq\log_{2}\frac{2\ln M}{-\ln(1-|\hat{S}|/M)}\leq\log_{2}\frac{2M\ln M}{|\hat{S}|}, $$

and $|\Delta|\leq 2^{d}\leq(2M\ln M)/|\hat{S}|$ . The total time complexity is $O(dM\log M)=\widetilde{O}(M)$ . ∎

Now we prove Theorem 4.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Apply Lemma 4.2 to set $S$ and in $|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}=|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ time obtain a modulus $M\in[|S|,|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}]$ such that $\hat{S}:=S\bmod M\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ has size $|\hat{S}|\geq|S|/2$ . Apply Lemma 4.2 to $\hat{S}$ and obtain set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time such that $\hat{S}+\Delta=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and $|\Delta|\leq O(\frac{M\log M}{|\hat{S}|})\leq O(\frac{M\log M}{|S|})\leq 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}$ . Compute the sumset $A+S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ in deterministic $O(|A+S|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ time via Lemma 2.1. Let $K=|A+S|/|S|$ .

#### Claim 4.4.

In $\widetilde{O}(KM+|C|)$ time, we can deterministically compute a partition of $C$ into $p=O(\log M)$ parts, $C=\bigcup_{i\in[p]}C^{(i)}$ , and shifts $\phi^{(0)},\dots,\phi^{(p-1)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , such that for every $i\in[p]$ ,

$$ (1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi^{(i)}})[c\bmod M]\leq O(K\log M)\text{ for all }c\in C^{(i)}. $$

#### Proof.

Compute the cyclic convolution $1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta}$ by brute force in $O(|A+S|\cdot|\Delta|)=O(KM\log M)$ time. We have

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}\big[(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[\hat{c}]\big]=|A+S||\Delta|/M. $$

By Markov’s inequality, the set

$$ \hat{C}_{\text{good}}:=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}:(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[\hat{c}]\leq 2|A+S||\Delta|/M\} $$

has size $|\hat{C}_{\text{good}}|\geq M/2$ . Then, we apply Lemma 4.3 to $\hat{C}_{\text{good}}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and compute in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time a set of shifts $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , $|\Phi|\leq O((M\log M)/|\hat{C}_{\text{good}}|)\leq O(\log M)$ , such that $\Phi+\hat{C}_{\text{good}}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ . So for every $\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ we can pick a shift $\varphi_{\hat{c}}\in\Phi$ such that $\hat{c}\in\varphi_{\hat{c}}+\hat{C}_{\text{good}}$ . Now we define a partition $C=\bigcup_{\phi\in\Phi}C_{\phi}$ where $C_{\phi}:=\{c\in C:\varphi_{c\bmod M}=\phi\}$ . Then, for all $c\in C_{\phi}$ , we have $(c\bmod M)-\phi\in\hat{C}_{\text{good}}$ , and hence

$$ (1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi})[c\bmod M]=(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[(c\bmod M)-\phi]\leq 2|A+S||\Delta|/M\leq O(K\log M). $$

Therefore, we can return $\{(C_{\phi},\phi)\}_{\phi\in\Phi}$ as the desired $\{(C^{(i)},\phi^{(i)})\}_{i\in[p]}$ , where $p=|\Phi|=O(\log M)$ . ∎

Let $\{(C^{(i)},\phi^{(i)})\}_{i\in[p]}$ (where $p=O(\log M)$ ) be returned by Claim 4.4. In the following, we will solve the #3SUM instance $(A,B,C^{(i)})$ separately for each $i\in[p]$ , i.e., we compute the desired answers defined in the statement of Theorem 4.1 but with $C^{(i)}$ replacing $C$ . Since $C$ is the disjoint union of all $C^{(i)}$ , in the end we can easily merge these answers over all $i\in[p]$ to get the answers for the original #3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ . This affects the total time complexity by at most a factor of $p=O(\log M)$ . From now on we focus on a particular pair of $C^{(i)}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and $\phi^{(i)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ .

Note that

$$ (S+\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\bmod M=\hat{S}+\Delta+\phi^{(i)}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}+\phi^{(i)}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}. $$

Hence, for every $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , there exists $s_{b}\in S$ such that $(b-s_{b})\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}$ . We pick such an $s_{b}$ for every $b\in B$ , in total time $\widetilde{O}(|S||\Delta+\phi^{(i)}|+|B|)=\widetilde{O}(M+|B|)$ time. Denote $d_{b}:=b-s_{b}$ , which satisfies

$$ d_{b}\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}. $$

Note that any 3SUM solution $(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C^{(i)}$ where $a+b=c$ must satisfy $d_{b}=(c-a)-s_{b}\in c-(A+S)$ . This motivates the definition of the set

$$ D_{c}:=\{d\in c-(A+S):d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}\} $$

for $c\in C^{(i)}$ . In this way, we can verify that the 3SUM solutions are decomposed into a disjoint union as follows (where we naturally define $B_{d}:=\{b\in B:d_{b}=d\},C_{d}:=\{c\in C^{(i)}:d\in D_{c}\}$ ),

$$ \{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C^{(i)}:a+b=c\}=\bigcup_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B_{d}\times C_{d}:a+b=c\}. $$

Note that $B_{d}\in d+S$ by the definition of $d_{b}$ .

Before describing our final #3SUM algorithm (which relies on the decomposition in Eq. 2), we first need to give size upper bounds for the sets $C_{d}$ , and show how to compute the sets $C_{d}$ efficiently.

#### Claim 4.5.

$\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|=O(|C|K\log M)$ .

#### Proof.

For $c\in C^{(i)}$ , by the definition of $D_{c}$ , we have

$$ |D_{c}|=\{x\in A+S:(c-x)\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}\}=(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi^{(i)}})[c\bmod M]\underset{\text{by \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eqn:forallcmultbound}}}{\leq}O(K\log M). $$

Then, $\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}}|C_{d}|=\sum_{c\in C^{(i)}}|D_{c}|\leq|C^{(i)}|\cdot O(K\log M)=O(|C|K\log M)$ . ∎

#### Claim 4.6.

We can compute all non-empty sets $C_{d}$ where $d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}$ , in time $\widetilde{O}(|C||\Delta|+|A+S|)$ in addition to the output size.

#### Proof.

Equivalently, we need to compute the sets $D_{c}$ for all $c\in C^{(i)}$ . To do this, by the definition of $D_{c}$ , it suffices to list all triples in the following set,

$$ \{(\hat{d},c,x)\in(\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\times C^{(i)}\times(A+S):\hat{d}=(c-x)\bmod M\}. $$

This can be viewed as listing all solutions in an instance of 3SUM modulo $M$ . It can be done by enumerating pairs $(\hat{d},c)\in(\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\times C^{(i)}$ and searching for $x\in A+S$ , in total time $\widetilde{O}(|\Delta||C^{(i)}|+|A+S|)\leq\widetilde{O}(|\Delta||C|+|A+S|)$ in addition to the output size. ∎

Now the #3SUM algorithm for $A,B,C^{(i)}$ works as follows based on the decomposition in Eq. 2: for every $d\in\mathbb{Z}$ for which $B_{d}\neq\emptyset$ and $C_{d}\neq\emptyset$ , we solve #3SUM on $A,B_{d},C_{d}$ in one of the two ways:

- 1. Enumerate pairs in $B_{d}\times C_{d}$ and searching in $A$ , in $\widetilde{O}(|B_{d}||C_{d}|)$ time (after initially preprocessing $A$ into a binary search tree), or,

- 2. Compute $1_{A}\star 1_{B_{d}}$ using sparse convolution (Lemma 2.1) and output $(1_{A}\star 1_{B_{d}})[c]$ for all $c\in C_{d}$ , and also compute $(1_{C_{d}}\star 1_{-B_{d}})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ using Lemma 2.2, both in time complexity $O((|C_{d}|+|A+B_{d}|)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)=O((|C_{d}|+|A+S|)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ deterministically, where we used $B_{d}\subseteq d+S$ .

We choose Item 1 if $|B_{d}|\leq X$ for some parameter $X\geq 1$ , otherwise choose Item 2. Then, the total time over all $d\in\mathbb{Z}$ is at most (ignoring $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ factors)

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:|B_{d}|\leq X}|B_{d}||C_{d}|+\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:|B_{d}|>X}(|C_{d}|+|A+S|) \displaystyle\leq X\cdot\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|+\frac{\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|B_{d}|}{X}\cdot|A+S|, $$

which can be balanced to

$$ \displaystyle O\Big(\sqrt{\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|B_{d}|\cdot|A+S|}\Big) \displaystyle=O\Big(\sqrt{(|C|K\log M)\cdot|B|\cdot K|S|}\Big), $$

so the time complexity becomes

$$ O\Big(K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)\Big). $$

To summarize, the total running time over all steps is (recall that $M\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ and $|\Delta|\leq N^{o(1)}$ )

$$ \displaystyle|A+S|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)+\widetilde{O}(KM+|C|)+\widetilde{O}(|C||\Delta|)+K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N) \displaystyle\leq(|A+S|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)}+K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N), $$

as claimed. ∎

## 5 Tool III: Almost Additive Hashing with Short Seed Length

In this section we design a small almost linear hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ that satisfies certain independence properties. Such hash family (with large size) was used in the randomized 3SUM reductions of [ABF23] and [JX23]. For our deterministic applications, we need to construct a hash family of small size, so that we can afford to enumerate all functions in the family.

Our construction is inspired by [ABF23] and [JX23], and additionally use the $\epsilon$ -biased sets of [AGHP92] to reduce the size of the family. After introducing this key ingredient in Section 5.1, we present the definitions and properties of our hash family $\mathcal{H}$ in Section 5.2. This hash family $\mathcal{H}$ will be later used in Section 6.1, Section 9.2, and Section 10.

### 5.1 Almost $k$ -wise independent distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$

As a key ingredient, we will use the almost $k$ -wise independent distribution with small sample space constructed by [AGHP92]. For our purposes, we need to generalize the binary case of [AGHP92] to the mod- $p$ case, following [BS00]. The prime $p$ will be chosen small enough to fit in a machine word, so that addition and multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ take constant time.

For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , let $\langle a,b\rangle\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ denote their inner product $\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}b_{i}$ .

We say a distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ is $\delta$ -almost uniform if it is at most $\delta$ away from the uniform distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ in $L_{1}$ distance. Let $\mu$ be a distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ . We say $\mu$ is $\delta$ -almost $k$ -wise independent, if for every coordinate subset $S\subseteq[m]$ of size $|S|=k^{\prime}\leq k$ , the marginal distribution of $\mu$ projected to the coordinates in $S$ is $\delta$ -almost uniform.

The following lemma summarizes the construction borrowed from [AGHP92, BS00], which will be used in the next section.

#### Lemma 5.1.

We can deterministically construct $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ of size $|\mathcal{C}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ in $\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time such that the following holds: Suppose we sample $c\in\mathcal{C}$ uniformly at random.

- 1. For any $k^{\prime}\leq k$ linearly independent vectors $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , the distribution of the $k^{\prime}$ -tuple $(\langle c,x_{1}\rangle),\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ is $\frac{1}{2p^{k-1}}$ -almost uniform.

- 2. For any $k^{\prime}<k$ vectors $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\dots=\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle=0]\geq\frac{1}{2p^{k^{\prime}}}$ .

In the following we explain how Lemma 5.1 follows from known results in [AGHP92, BS00].

For $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , define the Fourier coefficient $\mu(\gamma)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}}\mu(x)\omega_{p}^{-\langle\gamma,x\rangle}$ , where $\omega_{p}=e^{2\pi i/p}$ . We say a distribution $\mu$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $\epsilon$ -biased if $|\mu(\gamma)|\leq\epsilon$ for all $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$ .

#### Lemma 5.2 (e.g., [AGHP92, Corollary 1]).

Every $\epsilon$ -biased distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $p^{k/2}\epsilon$ -almost $k$ -wise independent.

The following construction of $\epsilon$ -biased distribution is a straightforward generalization of the powering construction from [AGHP92].

#### Lemma 5.3 ([AGHP92, Section 5]).

Let $\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{r}}$ be a finite field represented by a monic irreducible degree- $r$ polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , define their inner product $\langle a,b\rangle\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ by viewing $a,b$ as vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{r}$ .

When $(x,y)$ is uniformly drawn from $\mathbb{F}_{q}\times\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , the distribution of $(\langle 1,y\rangle,\langle x,y\rangle,\dots,\langle x^{m-1},y\rangle)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $\frac{m-1}{q}$ -biased.

#### Lemma 5.4.

For an $\epsilon$ -biased distribution $\mu$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , and an invertible matrix $M\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m\times m}$ , the distribution of $Mx\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ where $x\sim\mu$ is also $\epsilon$ -biased.

#### Proof.

The new distribution $M\mu$ has Fourier coefficients $\widehat{M\mu}(\gamma)=\mu(M^{\top}\gamma)$ (where $\gamma\neq\mathbf{0}$ ), which have magnitude at most $\epsilon$ since $\mu$ is $\epsilon$ -biased. ∎

Lemma 5.1 follows from putting the three lemmas together.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

We prove Item 1 first. Let $\delta=\frac{1}{2p^{k-1}}$ , and $\epsilon=\delta/p^{k/2}=\frac{1}{2p^{3k/2-1}}$ . Let $r:=\lceil\log_{p}\frac{m}{\epsilon}\rceil\leq\log_{p}(2m)+3k/2$ , and $q:=p^{r}\geq m/\epsilon$ . Construct the $\frac{m-1}{q}$ -biased (and hence $\epsilon$ -biased) set $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ from Lemma 5.3, which has size $|\mathcal{C}|=q^{2}=p^{2r}\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ , and can be computed in $|\mathcal{C}|\cdot m\cdot\widetilde{O}(r)=\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time (constructing the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{r}}$ takes $\widetilde{O}(r^{4}p^{1/2})$ time deterministically [Sho88], which is not a bottleneck). Now we verify that $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the claimed property. Fixing $k^{\prime}\leq k$ linearly independent $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , there is an invertible $m\times m$ matrix $M$ such that the first $k^{\prime}$ coordinates of $Mc$ for any $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ are $\langle c,x_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle$ . By Lemma 5.4, the distribution of $Mc$ where $c$ is uniformly drawn from $\mathcal{C}$ is also $\epsilon$ -biased, and hence $\delta$ -almost $k$ -wise independent by Lemma 5.2. In particular, the first $k^{\prime}$ coordinates of $Mc$ , $\langle c,x_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle$ , are $\delta$ -almost uniform. This concludes the proof of Item 1.

Now we derive Item 2 from Item 1. Pick any maximal linear independent subset of $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}$ , and without loss of generality assume it contains $x_{1},\dots,x_{r}$ . Since each $x_{j}$ is a linear combination of $x_{1},\dots,x_{r}$ , we have

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\cdots=\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle=0]=\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\cdots=\langle c,x_{r}\rangle=0]\underset{\text{by \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{item:dethashalmostuniform}}}{\geq}\tfrac{1}{p^{r}}-\delta\geq\tfrac{1}{p^{k^{\prime}}}-\tfrac{1}{2p^{k-1}}\geq\tfrac{1}{2p^{k^{\prime}}} $$

as claimed. ∎

### 5.2 Almost linear hashing with “almost” almost $k$ -wise independence

Let $k\geq 2$ be a fixed constant integer. We now construct our hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ . In the following we assume the universe size $N$ is larger than some big constant (possibly dependent on $k$ ) in order to simplify some calculation.

#### Definition 5.5 (Hash family $\mathcal{H}$ ).

Let $k\geq 2$ be a fixed constant integer. Given universe size $N$ and a prime parameter $p\geq\log^{2k}N$ , define a hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ as follows:

- • Let

$$ Q:=100\log N<p. $$

Deterministically pick distinct primes $q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{m-1}\in[Q/2,Q]$ such that

$$ q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{m-1}\in[N(\log N)^{2k},N(\log N)^{3k}], $$

(3) which is possible since the product of all primes in the interval $[50\log N,100\log N]$ is at least $N^{2}$ (by the Prime Number Theorem, e.g. [RS62]). In particular,

$$ m=(1+o(1))\tfrac{\log N}{\log\log N}. $$

- • Draw a random $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ from Lemma 5.1 with parameters $p,m,k$ . Then, for $x\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ , define vector $w=(x\bmod q_{1},x\bmod q_{2},\dots,x\bmod q_{m-1},1)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ (where each $x\bmod q_{i}$ is converted into $\{0,1,\dots,q_{i}-1\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}$ ), and let the hash value of $x$ be $h(x):=\langle c,w\rangle$ .

By Lemma 5.1, this hash family has size $|\mathcal{H}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ and can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time (the time for computing $q_{1},\dots,q_{m-1}$ is $O(logN)=o(p)$ and is negligible), and each hash function $h\in\mathcal{H}$ can be evaluated at any given $x$ in $O(m)=o(\log N)$ time.

First, we show that the hash family $\mathcal{H}$ is almost linear.

#### Lemma 5.6 (Almost linearity, $\Delta_{h}$ ).

In Definition 5.5, for every $h\in\mathcal{H}$ (defined using $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ ), we have $h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)\in\Delta_{h}$ for all $x,y\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ , where $\Delta_{h}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}$ is defined as the iterative sumset,

$$ \Delta_{h}:=\{0,-q_{1}c_{1}\}+\{0,-q_{2}c_{2}\}+\dots+\{0,-q_{m-1}c_{m-1}\}+c_{m} $$

with size $|\Delta_{h}|\leq 2^{m-1}=N^{o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $q_{i}\leq Q<p$ for all $i$ . For any $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)=c_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}c_{i}\cdot\big(((x+y)\bmod q_{i})-(x\bmod q_{i})-(y\bmod q_{i})\big). $$

By $((x+y)\bmod q_{i})-(x\bmod q_{i})-(y\bmod q_{i})\in\{0,-q_{i}\}$ , the claim immediately follows. ∎

Using almost linearity, we now show that the hash values of Sidon 4-tuples under $\mathcal{H}$ are highly correlated. Recall that for a set $\Delta$ , we define the iterative sumset $k\Delta=(k-1)\Delta+\Delta$ .

#### Lemma 5.7 (Hashing Sidon 4-tuples).

Suppose integers $x,y,z,w\in[N]$ satisfy $x+y=z+w$ . Then the hash family $\mathcal{H}$ from Definition 5.5 (with $k\geq 3$ ) satisfies

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\big[\exists i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:\{h(x),h(y),h(z),h(w)\}\subseteq i+\Delta^{\prime}_{h}\big]\geq\frac{1}{2p^{2}}, $$

where $\Delta^{\prime}_{h}:=3(\{0\}\cup\Delta_{h})\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , with size $|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|<(|\Delta_{h}|+1)^{3}\leq 2^{3m}=N^{o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

By the definition of $h$ and by Item 2 of Lemma 5.1, we have $h(x-y)=h(y-z)=0$ with at least $\frac{1}{2p^{2}}$ probability. Since $y-z=w-x$ , in this case we also have $h(w-x)=0$ . Then, by Lemma 5.6, we have $h(y)-h(z)\in\Delta_{h},h(x)-h(y)\in\Delta_{h}$ , and $h(w)-h(x)\in\Delta_{h}$ . So $h(y)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h},h(x)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}$ , and $h(w)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}$ . Then, for $i=h(z)$ , we have $\{h(x),h(y),h(z),h(w)\}\subseteq\{i\}\cup\{i+\Delta_{h}\}\cup\{i+2\Delta_{h}\}\cup\{i+3\Delta_{h}\}=i+\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . ∎

To state the next property of $\mathcal{H}$ , we need the following definition (which also appeared in [JX23]):

#### Definition 5.8 ( $k$ -term $\ell$ -relation).

We say $k$ integers $a_{1},\dots,a_{k}$ have a ( $k$ -term) $\ell$ -relation, if there exist integers $\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{k}\in[-\ell,\ell]$ such that $\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_{j}a_{j}=0$ , and at least one of $\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{k}$ is non-zero.

The following lemma states that the hash family $\mathcal{H}$ is almost $k$ -wise independent on integers without $\ell$ -relations for small $\ell$ .88 8 In contrast, on integers with $\ell$ -relations for small $\ell$ , the almost $k$ -wise independence must fail, as can be seen from Lemma 5.7.

#### Lemma 5.9 (“Almost” almost $k$ -wise independence).

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the hash family from Definition 5.5. Let $k^{\prime}\leq k$ , and integers $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ have no $2k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ -relations. Then,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\Big[h(x_{1})=h(x_{2})=\dots=h(x_{k^{\prime}})\Big]\leq p^{-(k^{\prime}-1)}\cdot 2(k+1)^{2}(2k+1)^{m-1}=p^{-(k^{\prime}-1)}N^{o(1)}. $$

We actually deduce Lemma 5.9 from the following lemma, which will also be useful in our applications.

#### Lemma 5.10.

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the hash family from Definition 5.5 (with fixed integer parameter $k$ ). Let $k^{\prime}\leq k-1$ , and integers $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ be such that $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}},0$ have no $(k^{\prime}+1)$ -term $k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ -relations. Then,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\Big[h(x_{i})\in\bigcup_{0\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq k}(k_{1}\Delta_{h}-k_{2}\Delta_{h})\text{ for all }1\leq i\leq k^{\prime}\Big]\leq p^{-k^{\prime}}\cdot 2(k+1)^{2}(2k+1)^{m-1}=p^{-k^{\prime}}N^{o(1)}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 5.10.

Suppose $h\in\mathcal{H}$ is specified by $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ . By the definition of $\Delta_{h}$ in Lemma 5.6, we know

$$ k_{1}\Delta_{h}-k_{2}\Delta_{h}=\Big\{(k_{1}-k_{2})c_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}x_{i}q_{i}c_{i}\,:\,x_{i}\in\{-k_{1},\dots,k_{2}\}\text{ for all }i\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}. $$

For $1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}$ , let $w_{j}:=(x_{j}\bmod q_{1},\dots,x_{j}\bmod q_{m-1},1)\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$ , and let $\widetilde{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ be $w_{j}$ with each coordinate viewed as an element in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Recall from Definition 5.5 that $h(x_{j})=\langle c,\widetilde{w}_{j}\rangle$ . Then, $h(x_{j})\in k_{1}\Delta_{h}-k_{2}\Delta_{h}$ if and only if

$$ (1+k_{2}-k_{1})c_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(\widetilde{w}_{j}-x_{i}q_{i})c_{i}=0\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. $$

for some $0\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq k$ and $(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})\in\{-k_{1},\dots,k_{2}\}^{m-1}$ . Now we fix $k_{1},k_{2}$ and $(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})$ , and later we will apply a union bound over all such possibilities (there are at most $(k+1)^{2}\cdot(2k+1)^{m-1}$ of them).

For each $1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}$ , define $u_{j}:=(w_{j}-x_{1}q_{1},w_{j}-x_{2}q_{2},\dots,w_{j}-x_{m-1}q_{m-1},1+k_{2}-k_{1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$ , and let $\widetilde{u}_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ be $u_{j}$ with each coordinate viewed as an element in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Then Eq. 4 is equivalent to $\langle c,\widetilde{u}_{j}\rangle=0\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

In the following we will prove that the vectors $\widetilde{u}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{u}_{k^{\prime}}$ are linearly independent. Once this is proved, Item 1 of Lemma 5.1 would imply that the distribution of $(\langle c,\widetilde{u}_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle c,\widetilde{u}_{m}\rangle)$ is $1/(2p^{k-1})$ -almost uniform, and in particular they are all zeros with probability at most $p^{-k^{\prime}}+1/(2p^{k-1})\leq 2p^{-k^{\prime}}$ . So, by a union bound over all $\leq(k+1)^{2}\cdot(2k+1)^{m-1}$ many possibilities of $k_{1},k_{2},(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})$ , we get the claimed probability upper bound in Lemma 5.10.

To prove $\widetilde{u}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{u}_{k^{\prime}}$ are linearly independent, we suppose for contradiction that they are linearly dependent. Define matrices $U:=\begin{pmatrix}|&|&&|\\ u_{1}&u_{2}&\cdots&u_{k^{\prime}}\\ |&|&&|\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times k^{\prime}}$ and $\widetilde{U}:=\begin{pmatrix}|&|&&|\\ \widetilde{u}_{1}&\widetilde{u}_{2}&\cdots&\widetilde{u}_{k^{\prime}}\\ |&|&&|\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m\times k^{\prime}}.$ Let $r<k^{\prime}$ be the rank of $\widetilde{U}$ . We pick a subset $R$ of $r$ rows and a subset $C$ of $r$ columns such that the submatrix $\widetilde{U}[R,C]$ has rank $r$ . Since $r<k^{\prime}$ , we can pick another column $c\in\{1,2,\dots,k^{\prime}\}\setminus C$ .

Now, we fix an arbitrary row $i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}$ . Observe that the $(r+1)\times(r+1)$ matrix $\widetilde{V}:=\begin{pmatrix}\widetilde{U}[R,C]&\widetilde{U}[R,c]\\ \widetilde{U}[i,C]&\widetilde{U}[i,c]\end{pmatrix}$ must have rank $r$ . This is because, if $i\notin R$ , then $\widetilde{V}$ is a submatrix of $\widetilde{U}$ , and cannot have rank larger than $r$ . Otherwise, $i\in R$ , so the last row of $\widetilde{V}$ repeats one of the previous $r$ rows. Hence, $\det\widetilde{V}=0\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , which means the integer matrix $V:=\begin{pmatrix}U[R,C]&U[R,c]\\ U[i,C]&U[i,c]\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant congruent to $0$ modulo $p$ . Since each entry in $V$ is an integer bounded by $(k+1)Q$ (by the definition of $u_{j}$ ), $\det V$ is an integer bounded by $(r+1)!((k+1)Q)^{r+1}\leq(k+1)^{2k}Q^{k}=O((\log N)^{k})$ , which is smaller than $p\geq\log^{2k}{N}$ assumed in Definition 5.5. Hence, from $\det V\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ we have $\det V=0$ . By expanding $\det V$ along the last row, we have (for notational convenience, assume $C\cup\{c\}=\{1,2,\dots,r+1\}$ without loss of generality)

$$ \sum_{j\in C\cup\{c\}}\underbrace{(-1)^{j}\det U[R,C\cup\{c\}\setminus\{j\}]}_{=:\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}}\cdot U[i,j]=0. $$

Here,

$$ |\beta_{j}|\leq r!((k+1)Q)^{r}\leq k^{2k}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}, $$

and

$$ \beta_{c}=(-1)^{c}\det U[R,C]\neq 0 $$

since $\widetilde{U}[R,C]$ is full-rank and so is $U[R,C]$ . We let $\beta_{j}=0$ for $j\notin C\cup\{c\}$ . Since row $i$ is arbitrary, Eq. 5 holds for all $1\leq i\leq m$ . For $i\leq m-1$ , recall $U[i,j]=w_{j}-x_{i}q_{i}\equiv x_{j}\pmod{q_{i}}$ , so Eq. 5 implies $\sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}\beta_{j}x_{j}\equiv 0\pmod{q_{i}}.$ Since

$$ \Big\lvert\sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}\beta_{j}x_{j}\Big\rvert\leq k^{\prime}\max_{j}|\beta_{j}|\cdot N\leq k^{\prime}k^{2k}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}N=O(N\log^{k^{\prime}-1}N), $$

which by Eq. 3 gives the upper bound $\lvert\sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}\beta_{j}x_{j}\rvert{<}q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{m-1}$ . Then, by Chinese Remainder Theorem with moduli $q_{1},\dots,q_{m-1}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}\beta_{j}x_{j}=0. $$

Set $\beta_{k^{\prime}+1}=-\sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}\beta_{j}$ , with $|\beta_{k^{\prime}+1}|\leq\sum_{1\leq j\leq k^{\prime}}|\beta_{j}|\leq k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ . Then, we have found a $(k^{\prime}+1)$ -term $k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ -relation for $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}},0$ with coefficients $\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{k^{\prime}+1}$ , a contradiction to the assumption that such relations do not exist. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.9 using Lemma 5.10.

By almost linearity Lemma 5.6 of $\mathcal{H}$ , we know $h(x_{i})=h(x_{j})$ implies $h(x_{i}-x_{j})\in-\Delta_{h}$ . So $h(x_{1})=\dots=h(x_{k^{\prime}})$ implies $h(x_{1}-x_{2}),h(x_{2}-x_{3}),\dots,h(x_{k^{\prime}-1}-x_{k^{\prime}})\in-\Delta_{h}$ . The probability that this happens can be bounded using Lemma 5.10 by at most $p^{-(k^{\prime}-1)}\cdot 2(k+1)^{2}(2k+1)^{m-1}$ , provided that we show $x_{1}-x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}-1}-x_{k^{\prime}},0$ have no $k^{\prime}$ -term $k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ -relations. To see this, note that if there is such a relation, then it immediately implies a $k^{\prime}$ -term $2k^{2k+1}Q^{k^{\prime}-1}$ -relation on $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}$ , contradicting our assumption. ∎

## 6 Tool IV: Deterministic BSG Theorem in Subquadratic Time

In this section, we prove the following deterministic algorithmic version of the BSG theorem running in subquadratic time when $K$ is not too small.

#### Theorem 6.1 (Full version of Theorem 1.11).

Given set $A\subseteq[N],r\geq 2$ and $K\geq 1$ such that $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , we can deterministically find subsets $A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\subseteq A$ in $O((|A|^{2}/K^{2r-4}+K^{13}|A|)N^{o(1)})$ time, such that

- • $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(64K)$ ,

- • $|B^{\prime}|\geq|A|/\big(K^{r+3}\cdot 2^{\frac{C\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\big)$ , and

- • $|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\leq K^{5}|A|\cdot 2^{\frac{C\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ ,

for some absolute constant $C\geq 1$ .

Note that Ruzsa triangle inequality implies $|A^{\prime}+A^{\prime}|\leq\frac{|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|^{2}}{|B^{\prime}|}\leq K^{13+r}|A|\cdot 2^{\frac{3C\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ .

### 6.1 Finding a small high-energy subset

The goal of this subsection is to prove the following theorem about finding a subset of appropriate size and high additive energy. This theorem will be used later for proving our derandomized subquadratic-time BSG theorem.

#### Theorem 6.2 (Finding a small high-energy subset).

Given set $A\subseteq[N]$ , size parameter $1\leq R\leq|A|$ , and $1\leq K\leq R^{1/3}$ such that $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ holds, in $O(K^{13}|A|N^{o(1)})$ time we can deterministically find a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ such that

$$ \mathsf{E}(A^{\prime})\geq\frac{|A^{\prime}|^{3}}{K}\cdot 2^{-\frac{C\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}, $$

and

$$ \frac{R}{K^{2}}\leq|A^{\prime}|\leq R\cdot 2^{\frac{C\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}, $$

where $C\geq 1$ is some absolute constant.

Theorem 6.2 follows from iterating the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.3.

Assume $N\geq N_{0}$ for some absolute constant $N_{0}>1$ . Given set $A\subseteq[N]$ and $1\leq K\leq|A|^{1/3}\cdot 2^{-\frac{3\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ such that $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ holds, in $O(K^{13}|A|N^{o(1)})$ time we can deterministically find a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ such that

$$ \mathsf{E}(A^{\prime})\geq\frac{|A^{\prime}|^{3}}{K}\cdot 2^{-\frac{700\log N}{\log\log N}} $$

and

$$ \frac{|A|}{K^{2}}\cdot 2^{-\frac{3\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\leq|A^{\prime}|\leq|A|\cdot 2^{-\frac{\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 6.2 using Lemma 6.3.

If $N=O(1)$ then $|A|=O(1)$ , and we can simply return $A$ which satisfies the requirements for large enough $C\geq 1$ . Hence, in the following we assume $N$ is large enough in order to simplify calculation.

Let $A_{0}=A,K_{0}=K$ . In iteration $i$ ( $i\geq 0$ ):

- • If $|A_{i}|\leq R\cdot 2^{\frac{2109\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ , then return $A_{i}$ as our answer $A^{\prime}$ .

- • Otherwise, apply Lemma 6.3 to $A_{i}$ and $K_{i}$ , and let $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_{i}$ be the returned subset, and let $K_{i+1}=K_{i}\cdot 2^{\frac{700\log N}{\log\log N}}$ .

We now verify the conditions required by Lemma 6.3 are satisfied. By the energy bound in Lemma 6.3, we have $\mathsf{E}(A_{i+1})\geq|A_{i+1}|^{3}/K_{i+1}$ . By the size bound in Lemma 6.3, $|A_{i+1}|/|A_{i}|\leq 2^{-\frac{\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ , so the algorithm terminates in at most $\sqrt{\log\log N}$ iterations before the size of $A_{i}$ drops below $1$ . Hence,

$$ K_{i}=K2^{\frac{700\log N}{\log\log N}\cdot i}\leq K2^{\frac{700\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\leq R^{1/3}2^{\frac{700\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}<\big(|A_{i}|2^{\frac{-2109\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\big)^{1/3}2^{\frac{700\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}=|A_{i}|^{1/3}2^{\frac{-3\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}, $$

satisfying the conditions required by Lemma 6.3.

Now we show the returned subset $A_{i}\subseteq A$ satisfies the claimed properties. If the returned subset is $A_{0}=A$ then clearly all requirements are satisfied, so we assume $i\geq 1$ . Then, $|A_{i-1}|>R\cdot 2^{\frac{2109\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\geq|A_{i}|$ , so by the size bound of Lemma 6.3 we have $|A_{i}|\geq\frac{|A_{i-1}|}{K_{i-1}^{2}}\cdot 2^{-\frac{3\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}>\frac{R\cdot 2^{\frac{2109\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}}{(K\cdot 2^{\frac{700\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}})^{2}}\cdot 2^{-\frac{3\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}\geq\frac{R}{K^{2}}$ as desired. The energy bound of Lemma 6.3 gives $\mathsf{E}(A_{i})\geq\frac{|A_{i}|^{3}}{K_{i-1}}\cdot 2^{-\frac{700\log N}{\log\log N}}\geq\frac{|A_{i}|^{3}}{K\cdot 2^{\frac{700\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}}\cdot 2^{-\frac{700\log N}{\log\log N}}\geq\frac{|A_{i}|^{3}}{K}\cdot 2^{-\frac{701\log N}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}}$ as desired.

The total time complexity over the at most $\sqrt{\log\log N}$ iterations is still $O(K^{13}|A|N^{o(1)})$ . This concludes the proof. ∎

In the rest of this subsection, we prove Lemma 6.3. in $O((|A|+k|B|)N^{o(1)})$ time, where $|\widetilde{S}|\leq\frac{|A||B|}{|A|/2k}=2k|B|$ . Our goal is to exactly compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}$ .

For every $1\leq i\leq g$ , use Theorem 1.9 to deterministically approximate $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}$ up to additive error $\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ , in time $\widetilde{O}((k|B|+|A_{i}|)N^{o(1)})$ , and total time $O((Kk|B|+|A|)N^{o(1)})$ for all $1\leq i\leq g$ . Then we define a partition $\widetilde{S}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cdots\cup S_{g}\cup\hat{S}$ as follows: for each $s\in\widetilde{S}$ , pick an arbitrary $1\leq i\leq g$ such that the approximate value of $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]$ is at least $\frac{|A_{i}|}{6k}$ (so that the real value satisfies $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ ), and put $s$ in $S_{i}$ . If no such $i$ exists, then put $s$ in $\hat{S}$ . Note that every $s\in\hat{S}$ satisfies

$$ (1_{\hat{A}}\star 1_{B})[s]=(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]-\sum_{i=1}^{g}(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A|}{2k}-\sum_{i=1}^{g}(\frac{|A_{i}|}{6k}+\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k})\geq\frac{|A|}{4k}. $$

We have the following claims:

#### Claim 7.1.

For all $1\leq i\leq g$ , $|S_{i}+B_{i}|\leq O(kK^{6}|B|N^{o(1)})$ .

#### Proof.

For any $s\in S_{i},b\in B_{i}$ , there are at least $(1_{A_{i}}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ many distinct representations of $s+b=(s-a)+(a+b)$ such that $a\in A_{i},s-a\in B$ , $a+b\in A_{i}+B_{i}$ . Hence, $(1_{B}\star 1_{A_{i}+B_{i}})[s+b]\geq\frac{|A_{i}|}{12k}$ . Therefore, $|S_{i}+B_{i}|\leq\frac{|B|\cdot|A_{i}+B_{i}|}{|A_{i}|/(12k)}\leq 12k|B|\cdot 64K^{6}N^{o(1)}$ , where the last step uses Eq. 17. ∎

We use Theorem 4.1 (applied to $(A,B,C,S):=(S_{i},-B,A,B_{i})$ ) to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in S_{i}$ , in time complexity

$$ \displaystyle O\Big(\frac{|S_{i}+B_{i}|\sqrt{|-B||A|}}{\sqrt{|B_{i}|}}\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\leq O\Big(\frac{kK^{6}|B|\sqrt{|B||A|}}{\sqrt{\frac{|A|}{K^{1/3}}/K^{6}}}\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\leq O(|B|^{1.5}kK^{55/6}N^{o(1)}). $$

Summing over all $1\leq i\leq g$ , the total time is $O(|B|^{1.5}kK^{61/6}N^{o(1)})$ .

#### Claim 7.2.

$|\hat{S}|\leq O\left(k^{2}\sqrt{\frac{|B|^{3}}{K|A|}}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

By Eq. 18,

$$ |\hat{S}|\cdot\left(\frac{|A|}{4k}\right)^{2}\leq\sum_{s\in\hat{S}}((1_{\hat{A}}\star 1_{B})[s])^{2}\leq\mathsf{E}(\hat{A},B)\leq\sqrt{\mathsf{E}(\hat{A})\mathsf{E}(B)}\leq\sqrt{\frac{2|A|^{3}}{K}\cdot|B|^{3}}, $$

so $|\hat{S}|\leq O\left(k^{2}\sqrt{\frac{|B|^{3}}{K|A|}}\right)$ . ∎

We use brute force to compute $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\hat{S}$ , in $\widetilde{O}(|B|+|\hat{S}||A|)=\widetilde{O}(k^{2}\sqrt{|A||B|^{3}/K})$ time.

Therefore, we have computed $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in\widetilde{S}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cdots\cup S_{g}\cup\hat{S}$ , in total time

$$ O\Big(\Big((|A|^{2}/K+K^{14}|A|)+(|B|^{1.5}kK^{61/6})+k^{2}\sqrt{|A||B|^{3}/K}\Big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big) $$

By setting $K=|A|^{3/64}$ , the total time becomes

$$ O\Big((|A|^{2-3/64}+k^{2}|B|^{1.5}|A|^{61/128})\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big)\leq O(k^{2}\cdot|A|^{2-3/128}N^{o(1)}). $$

∎

## 8 Deterministic Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances

We use our deterministic approximate 3SUM-counting algorithm (Theorem 1.9) to show an $O(nm^{o(1)}/\epsilon)$ -time deterministic algorithm for $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances, proving Theorem 1.4.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Let $T[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}n]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ denote the input text and pattern strings over an alphabet $\Sigma$ . By dividing $T$ into $O(n/m)$ chunks, we can assume $n=O(m)$ without loss of generality.

We start by describing a very simple $\epsilon m$ -additive approximation algorithm. For each symbol $s\in\Sigma$ , let $A_{s}:=\{j:T[j]=s\}$ and $B_{s}:=\{k:P[k]=s\}$ . Then the Hamming distance between $T[i+1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}i+m]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ can be expressed as

$$ |P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})[i]. $$

For each $s\in\Sigma$ , use Theorem 1.9 to compute in $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot m^{o(1)})$ time a sparse vector $f_{s}$ such that $\|f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B_{s}|$ . The total time complexity is $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}\sum_{s\in\Sigma}|A_{s}|+\sum_{s\in\Sigma}|B_{s}|)\cdot m^{o(1)})=\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ . Then, sum up the vectors $f_{s}$ over $s\in\Sigma$ , and output $|P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}f_{s}[i]$ as our approximation for the Hamming distance at shift $i$ , which clearly has additive error at most $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\big\lvert\big(f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\big)[i]\big\rvert\leq\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\epsilon|B_{s}|=\epsilon m$ .

This algorithm already achieves $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximation for distances that are $\Theta(m)$ , but in general we still need to handle smaller distances $\Theta(k)$ and achieve better additive error $O(\epsilon k)$ for them. Similarly to [CJVX23, Lemma 3.5], we handle this using the technique of Gawrychowski and Uznański [GU18], which reduced $k$ -bounded Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances to the special case where both text and pattern strings have run-length encodings bounded by $O(k)$ (i.e., they are concatenations of $O(k)$ blocks of identical characters). This reduction runs in near-linear time, and preserves additive approximation. In the following we show how to approximate $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ with $O(\epsilon k)$ coordinate-wise additive error in this special case in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ time, from which the theorem follows.

Now each $A_{s},B_{s}$ is a union of blocks (intervals), and there are $O(k)$ blocks in total over all symbols $s\in\Sigma$ . Since these $O(k)$ blocks have total length $O(m)$ , we can assume each block has length $O(m/k)$ (by possibly breaking up longer blocks). Then, we use the same strategy as [CJVX23, Lemma 3.5] and assume each block is dyadic (i.e., it takes the form $\{z\cdot 2^{u},z\cdot 2^{u}+1,\dots,(z+1)\cdot 2^{u}-1\}$ for some integers $z,u\geq 0$ ), by breaking up each original block into at most $2\log(m/k)+O(1)$ blocks; the total number of blocks becomes $O(k\log m)$ . For $s\in\Sigma$ and $1\leq 2^{u}\leq O(m/k)$ , define set $A^{u}_{s}$ as the left endpoints of $2^{u}$ -length blocks in $A_{s}$ , and define $B^{u}_{s}$ similarly. In particular, $1_{A_{s}}=\sum_{u}(1_{A^{u}_{s}}\star 1_{\{0,1,\dots,2^{u}-1\}})$ . We can decompose $(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ into the sum of contribution from pairs of blocks, and obtain

$$ \sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})=\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\sum_{u,v}1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\star\underbrace{1_{\{0,\dots,2^{u}-1\}}\star 1_{-\{0,\dots,2^{v}-1\}}}_{=:L_{u,v}}. $$

For each $s,u,v$ , we use Theorem 1.9 to compute $f_{s,u,v}$ such that $\|f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\epsilon k}{m}|B_{s}^{v}|$ , in $O\big(\big((\epsilon^{-1}m/k)|A_{s}^{u}|+|B_{s}^{v}|\big)\cdot m^{o(1)}\big)$ time. The total time complexity over all $s,u,v$ is $O(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ since $\sum_{u,s}|A_{s}^{u}|,\sum_{v,s}|B_{s}^{v}|\leq O(k\log m)$ and $u,v\leq O(\log m)$ . When $u\geq v$ (the $u<v$ case is symmetric), $L_{u,v}$ is a multiset with multiplicity at most $2^{v}$ and supported on an interval of length $<2\cdot 2^{u}$ , and $A_{s}^{u}$ and $B_{s}^{v}$ only contain multiples of $2^{v}$ , so for any $i$ the absolute difference between $(1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\star L_{u,v})[i]$ and $(f_{s,u,v}\star L_{u,v})[i]$ (WLOG assuming $f_{s,u,v}$ is only supported on multiples of $2^{v}$ ) is at most

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j}\big\lvert(f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}})[j]\big\rvert\cdot L_{u,v}[i-j] \displaystyle\leq\frac{2\cdot 2^{u}}{2^{v}}\|f_{s,u,v}-1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}\|_{\infty}\|L_{u,v}\|_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2\cdot 2^{u}}{2^{v}}\cdot\frac{\epsilon k}{m}|B_{s}^{v}|\cdot 2^{v} \displaystyle=O(\epsilon|B_{s}^{v}|). $$

Hence, if we use $f_{s,u,v}$ to replace $1_{A_{s}^{u}}\star 1_{-B_{s}^{v}}$ in Eq. 19 and compute the summation using FFT in $\widetilde{O}(m)$ time, we can obtain an approximation of $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})$ with coordinate-wise additive error $\sum_{s,u,v}O(\epsilon|B_{s}^{v}|)\leq O(\epsilon k\log^{2}m)$ . This error can be made $O(\epsilon k)$ by suitably decreasing $\epsilon$ . The total time complexity is $O(\epsilon^{-1}m^{1+o(1)})$ . ∎

## 9 Deterministic 3SUM Reductions

In this section, we prove the deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with small additive energy Theorem 1.1. The overall framework is the same as previous randomized reductions in [ABF23, JX23], but here we need to make everything deterministic, by combining the derandomized versions of the BSG theorem, the small-doubling 3SUM algorithm, and the derandomized almost additive hashing from previous sections.

### 9.1 From high-energy to moderate-energy

Throughout this section, we consider the following version of 3SUM: given $A\subset\{-n^{3},\dots,n^{3}\}$ of size $|A|=n$ , determine if there exists $(a,b,c)\in A\times A\times A$ such that $a+b+c=0$ .99 9 The case where $A$ comes from a larger universe can be deterministically reduced to this version by [FKP24, Theorem 1.2]. The additive energy of the 3SUM instance is $n^{2}<\mathsf{E}(A)<n^{3}$ .

#### Lemma 9.1.

There is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2.95}$ .

#### Proof.

The randomized version of this reduction was already given by [ABF23] and [JX23] using a randomized algorithmic version of the BSG theorem. Our derandomized version follows the same idea, except that we need to use the deterministic BSG theorem and deterministic energy approximation algorithm.

Let $A_{0}$ denote the 3SUM instance, $|A_{0}|=n$ . Let $K=n^{0.05}$ . Maintain a subset $A\subseteq A_{0}$ , which initially equals $A_{0}$ . We iteratively proceed as follows. In each iteration:

- 1. If $|A|\leq n^{0.9}$ , then solve 3SUM on $A$ in $O(|A|^{2})=O(n^{1.8})$ time, and return the 3SUM answer.

- 2. Use Corollary 3.4 to deterministically approximate $\mathsf{E}(A)$ up to additive error $\frac{|A|^{3}}{3K}$ , in $O(K|A|n^{o(1)})$ time. If the approximate value is at most $\frac{2|A|^{3}}{3K}$ , then we know $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq|A|^{3}/K\leq|A|^{2.95}$ , and we can use the moderate-energy 3SUM solver to solve $A$ , and return the 3SUM answer.

- 3. Otherwise, we have $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq\frac{|A|^{3}}{3K}$ . We apply the deterministic BSG algorithm (Theorem 6.1 with $r=3$ ) to $A$ with parameter $3K$ , and in $O(|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)\cdot n^{o(1)}$ time we can obtain $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ of size $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(192K)$ and another set $B^{\prime}$ such that $|B^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(K^{6}n^{o(1)}),|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\leq K^{5}|A|n^{o(1)}$ . We then use Theorem 4.1 (applied to $(A,B,C,S):=(A^{\prime},A,-A,B^{\prime})$ ) to decide whether $(1_{-A}\star 1_{-A})[a]>0$ for some $a\in A^{\prime}$ (i.e., there exists $(a,b,c)\in A^{\prime}\times A\times A$ such that $-b-c=a$ ), in time complexity $\displaystyle O\Big(\frac{|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\sqrt{|A||A|}}{\sqrt{|B^{\prime}|}}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)+\big(|A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|+|A|\big)\cdot n^{o(1)}\Big)$ $\displaystyle=O((\frac{K^{5}|A|^{2}}{\sqrt{|A|/K^{6}}}+K^{5}|A|)n^{o(1)})$ $\displaystyle=O(K^{8}|A|^{1.5}n^{o(1)}).$ If a 3SUM solution is found, then we return and terminate. Otherwise, we know $A$ has no 3SUM solutions that involve numbers in $A^{\prime}$ , so we can remove $A^{\prime}$ and let $A\leftarrow A\setminus A^{\prime}$ , and proceed to the next iteration.

Since $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(192K)$ , each iteration decreases $|A|$ to at most $(1-1/(192K))|A|$ , so the number of iteration before $|A|$ drops below $n^{0.9}$ is at most $O(K\log n)$ . The time complexity in each iteration is

$$ O(K|A|n^{o(1)})+O((|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)n^{o(1)})+O(K^{8}|A|^{1.5}n^{o(1)}), $$

so over all $O(K\log n)$ iterations, the total time is at most

$$ n^{o(1)}\cdot O(K^{14}n+K^{9}n^{1.5}+n^{2}/K)\leq O(n^{1.95+o(1)}). $$

So the time complexity of this reduction is truly subquadratic. ∎

### 9.2 From moderate-energy to low-energy

In this section, we use our almost additive hash family $\mathcal{H}$ from Definition 5.5 and the deterministic energy approximation algorithm (Corollary 3.4) to show the following fine-grained reduction:

#### Lemma 9.2.

Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ be a fixed constant. There is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\alpha}$ to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\beta}$ , where $\beta=\alpha-\alpha(1-\alpha)/30\in(0,\alpha)$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose all 3SUM instances of additive energy at most $n^{2+\beta}$ can be solved in $n^{2-\delta}$ time for some $\delta>0$ .

Let $A\subset[N]$ be the input 3SUM instance with $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq|A|^{2+\alpha}$ , with $|A|=n$ , $N=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(n)$ . We will perform the standard 3SUM self-reduction using the hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ from Lemma 5.1, with parameter $k=3$ , and prime $2\leq p<|A|$ to be determined later.

By almost linearity of $\mathcal{H}$ (Lemma 5.6), any 3SUM solution $a+b+c=0$ satisfies $h(0)-h(a)-h(b+c)\in\Delta_{h}$ and $h(b+c)-h(b)-h(c)\in\Delta_{h}$ , so $h(a)+h(b)+h(c)\in h(a)+h(b+c)-\Delta_{h}\in h(0)-2\Delta_{h}$ . For $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , let $h^{-1}(i)=\{x\in\{-N,\dots,N\}:h(x)=i\}$ . Define $\Delta^{\prime}_{h}=h(0)-2\Delta_{h}$ which has size $|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|\leq|\Delta_{h}|^{2}=n^{o(1)}$ . So in order to solve the original 3SUM instance, we only need to solve the smaller 3-partite 3SUM instances $\big(h^{-1}(i)\cap A,h^{-1}(j)\cap A,h^{-1}(k)\cap A\big)$ , where $i+j+k\in\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . (There are $p\cdot p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|=p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ such instances.)

We need to reduce these 3-partite 3SUM instances back to the one-partite version that we are working with, as follows: suppose $X,Y,Z\subseteq\{-N,\dots,N\}$ are the three input sets of the 3-partite 3SUM. we define set $W=(X+30N)\cup(Y+100N)\cup(Z-130N)$ as the one-partite 3SUM instance. Note that any original 3SUM solution $(x,y,z)\in X\times Y\times Z$ , $x+y+z=0$ implies a solution $(x+30N)+(y+100N)+(z-130N)=0$ in the new instance. One can verify that, conversely, any 3SUM solution in $W$ correspond to an original solution, due to the way we shifted the sets. Furthermore, we can similarly verify that any Sidon 4-tuple in $W$ can be divided into two pairs, $(a,b),(c,d)$ , where $a-b=c-d$ , and the two numbers in each pair come from the same part ( $X+30N$ , $Y+100N$ , or $Z-130N$ ). So it actually corresponds to a (shifted) Sidon 4-tuple from the original instance in $X,Y,Z,$ or between $X,Y$ , between $Y,Z$ , or between $Z,X$ . This means the new one-partite 3SUM instance $W$ has additive energy

$$ \mathsf{E}(W)=\mathsf{E}(X)+\mathsf{E}(Y)+\mathsf{E}(Z)+\mathsf{E}(X,Y)+\mathsf{E}(Y,Z)+\mathsf{E}(Z,X). $$

Our goal is to deterministically pick a $h\in\mathcal{H}$ to perform the 3SUM self-reduction mentioned above, so that the produced instances have low total additive energy. To do this, we try every $h\in\mathcal{H}$ , and check whether $h$ is good. Recall from Definition 5.5 that $|\mathcal{H}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{12}$ .

We first need to analyze the expected total energy of the produced instances under a random $h\in\mathcal{H}$ . To do this, we consider each individual Sidon 4-tuple in $A$ , $a+b=c+d$ , and analyze its expected contribution to the total energy of all produced instances. Given the discussion above, the contribution of this 4-tuple to the total energy (under a specific $h\in\mathcal{H}$ ) is determined as follows:

- • If $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)=i^{*}$ for some $i^{*}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , then they are hashed to the same bucket $i^{*}$ , and it corresponds to a Sidon 4-tuple in every instance $\big(h^{-1}(i^{*})\cap A,h^{-1}(j)\cap A,h^{-1}(k)\cap A\big)$ , where $i^{*}+j+k\in\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . There are $O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ such choices of $j,k$ , so this Sidon 4-tuple contributes $O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ to the total energy.

- • If $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are not distinct but not all equal, then by a similar reasoning, this Sidon 4-tuple can contribute at most $O(|\Delta^{\prime}|)$ to the total energy.

- • If $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are distinct, then they are hashed to four different buckets, and hence do not contribute to the total energy.

Now we can analyze the expected contribution of the Sidon 4-tuple $a+b=c+d$ to the total energy, by distinguishing several cases:

- • if $a=b=c=d$ , then clearly $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)$ . There are only $|A|$ such 4-tuples.

- • Otherwise, there are at least two distinct values among $a,b,c,d$ . Say they are $a,b$ . Note that $a\neq b$ cannot have any $2$ -term $\ell$ -relation as defined in Definition 5.8, so by Lemma 5.9 we know $h(a)=h(b)$ happens with at most $n^{o(1)}/p$ probability. Now we look at more subcases. – If $a,b,c$ has no $O(Q^{2})$ -relation, then by Lemma 5.9, $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)$ happens with probability at most $n^{o(1)}/p^{2}$ . The number of such 4-tuples are trivially upper-bounded by $\mathsf{E}(A)$ . – Otherwise, $a,b,c$ has a $O(Q^{2})$ -relation. Then there are at most $(O(Q^{2}))^{2}-1=n^{o(1)}$ ways to pick the coefficients $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=0$ of this relation, and there are $|A|^{2}$ possibilities for $(a,b)\in A^{2}$ , which then uniquely determine $c$ by the relation $\beta_{1}a+\beta_{2}b+\beta_{3}c=0$ , and then uniquely determine $d$ by $a+b=c+d$ . Hence, in total there are at most $n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}$ such 4-tuples.

Hence, the expected number of tuples $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ such that $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)=h(d)$ can be bounded by $|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p^{2}+n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p$ . The expected number of $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ such that $h(a),h(b),h(c),h(d)$ are not distinct can be bounded by $|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p$ . Together, their contribution to the total energy of all instances is in expectation

$$ \displaystyle\big(|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p^{2}+n^{o(1)}|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p\big)\cdot O(p\cdot|\Delta^{\prime}|)+\big(|A|+\mathsf{E}(A)\cdot n^{o(1)}/p\big)\cdot O(|\Delta^{\prime}|) \displaystyle=O((|A|p+\mathsf{E}(A)/p+|A|^{2})\cdot n^{o(1)}). $$

We can also use a similar (and simpler) argument to bound the expected total squared size of the buckets, by

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\Big[\sum_{i}|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|^{2}\Big]\leq O(|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p). $$

By Markov’s inequality and a union bound, we know there is an $h\in\mathcal{H}$ such that both upper bounds Eqs. 20 and 21 hold (up to a constant factor) without taking expectation. The goal is to find such $h$ (or any other good enough $h$ ), by enumerating $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and checking whether $h$ is good deterministically.

Let $\epsilon>0$ be some constant to be determined later. For each $h\in\mathcal{H}$ , do the following steps:

- • If the bound in Eq. 21 is violated for $h$ then we terminate this procedure and start to check the next hash function. Otherwise, use $h$ to perform the 3SUM self-reduction described above and obtain $p^{2}|\Delta^{\prime}|=p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ smaller 3SUM instances.

- • All instances of size $<|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p$ are marked as light. All buckets of size $|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|\geq\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ are marked as heavy. All instances that include at least one heavy buckets are marked as heavy.

- • Let $\mu:=|A|^{\alpha-1-4\epsilon}$ . For each non-heavy instance (which can have size $\leq|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ ), use Corollary 3.4 to approximate its additive energy up to additive error $\mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}=|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon}/p^{3}$ . If the approximate energy is greater than $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ , then mark this instance as high-energy. The total time of this step over all $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ instances is $p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot O(\mu^{-1}\cdot|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\cdot n^{o(1)})=p|A|^{2-\alpha+5\epsilon+o(1)}$ .

- • If the sum of the approximate energy (from the previous step) over all non-heavy instances is greater than $|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , then $h$ is bad, and we terminate this procedure and start to check the next hash function. Otherwise, we declare $h$ as good, and we will not try other hash functions any more. The following steps are only run for the good $h$ .

- • We solve all light, and high-energy instances by brute force in quadratic time. For each item $a\in A$ landing in a heavy bucket, use $\widetilde{O}(|A|)$ time to find 3SUM solutions involving it.

- • For each remaining instance that is non-heavy, it has size $s\in[|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p,|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p]$ , and has additive energy at most $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}+\mu\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\leq|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ . We will set parameters later so that

$$ |A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}\leq(|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p)^{2+\beta} $$

holds, which is equivalent to

$$ |A|^{\alpha+(6+\beta)\epsilon-\beta}\leq p^{1-\beta}. $$

(22) Then this instance has additive energy at most $s^{2+\beta}$ , and hence can be solved in $s^{2-\delta}$ time by assumption.

To show the correctness of this reduction, we need to show at least one $h$ is good. Note that when estimating the total additive energy of all $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ instances, the total additive error incurred is

$$ \mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\cdot p^{2}n^{o(1)}=|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p. $$

By Eq. 20 we know there is some $h$ such that the total energy is at most

$$ O((|A|^{2}+|A|^{2+\alpha}/p))\cdot n^{o(1)}\leq O(|A|^{2+\alpha+o(1)}/p). $$

For such $h$ , the approximate total energy is at most $O(|A|^{2+\alpha+o(1)}/p)+|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p\leq|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , so our algorithm will declare this $h$ as good. On the other hand, if we declare some $h$ as good, then we know the total additive energy of all non-heavy instances is at most $|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p+|A|^{2+\alpha-\epsilon+o(1)}/p\leq 2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ .

Now it remains to analyze the time complexity of the whole algorithm.

- • The energy estimation step takes $p|A|^{2-\alpha+5\epsilon+o(1)}$ time for each $h\in\mathcal{H}$ . We need to enumerate all $h\in\mathcal{H}$ (where $|\mathcal{H}|\leq n^{o(1)}p^{12})$ , so the total time is

$$ p^{13}|A|^{2+5\epsilon-\alpha+o(1)}. $$

(23)

- • By Eq. 21, the total size of heavy buckets $i$ (that is, with size $|h^{-1}(i)\cap A|\geq\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p$ ) is at most $O(|A|^{2}\cdot n^{o(1)}/p)/\big(\frac{1}{3}|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)\leq O(|A|^{1-\epsilon+o(1)})$ . For each of them we spend $\widetilde{O}(|A|)$ time to find 3SUM solutions involving it, which is $O(|A|^{2-\epsilon+o(1)})$ total time.

- • The total time for solving (at most $p^{2}n^{o(1)}$ many) light instances is $p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot\big(|A|^{1-\epsilon}/p\big)^{2}=|A|^{2-2\epsilon+o(1)}$ .

- • Since the total additive energy of all non-heavy instances is $\leq 2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p$ , the number of instances with that are marked as high-energy (which should have energy at least $0.5|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}-\mu\cdot\big(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p\big)^{3}\geq 0.4|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}$ ) is at most $\frac{2|A|^{2+\alpha+\epsilon}/p}{0.4|A|^{2+\alpha+4\epsilon}/p^{3}}=5p^{2}/|A|^{3\epsilon}$ . The total time for solving these high-energy non-heavy instances is at most $\big(5p^{2}/|A|^{3\epsilon}\big)\cdot O((|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p)^{2})\leq O(|A|^{2-\epsilon+o(1)})$ .

- • The remaining instances are solved by the assumed subquadratic-time algorithm on lower energy instances. The total time is

$$ p^{2}n^{o(1)}\cdot(|A|^{1+\epsilon}/p)^{2-\delta} $$

(24)

The remaining goal is to set parameters $\beta\in(0,\alpha),p$ , and $\epsilon>0$ , so that Eq. 22 holds, and Eqs. 23 and 24 are truly-subquadratic in $|A|$ . This is achieved by setting

$$ \displaystyle\beta \displaystyle=\alpha-\alpha(1-\alpha)/30, \displaystyle p \displaystyle=\Theta(|A|^{\alpha/15}), $$

and $\epsilon>0$ small enough (in particular, $\epsilon:=\min\{\alpha(1-\alpha)/420,\delta/100\}$ ). To verify, note that Eq. 22 holds because

$$ |A|^{\alpha+(6+\beta)\epsilon-\beta}=|A|^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/30+(6+\beta)\epsilon}\leq|A|^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/20}=\Theta(p^{0.75(1-\alpha)}), $$

whereas $p^{1-\beta}=p^{(1-\alpha)(1+\alpha/30)}\geq p^{0.75(1-\alpha)}$ . Eq. 23 can be upper-bounded by

$$ |A|^{13\alpha/15}\cdot|A|^{2+5\epsilon-\alpha+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2+5\epsilon-2\alpha/15+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2-\alpha/15+o(1)}. $$

And Eq. 24 can be upper-bounded by $|A|^{(1+\epsilon)(2-\delta)+o(1)}p^{\delta}\leq|A|^{2+2\epsilon-\delta+\delta\alpha/15+o(1)}\leq|A|^{2-0.9\delta+o(1)}$ . ∎

Now we can prove Theorem 1.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

For any given constant $\delta>0$ , we deterministically reduce from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ as follows: first apply Lemma 9.1 to reduce from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2.95}$ . Then, starting with $\alpha_{0}:=0.95$ , repeatedly apply Lemma 9.2 to reduce from 3SUM with additive energy at most $\alpha_{i}$ to 3SUM with additive energy at most $\alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{i}(1-\alpha_{i})/30$ . One can check that the sequences $\{\alpha_{i}\}$ converges to $0$ . Hence, there is some step where we arrive at 3SUM instances of additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ as desired.

Recall that we initially start from 3SUM with universe $O(n^{3})$ (which is allowed by [FKP24, Theorem 1.2]). There are only finitely many steps of reductions. In each step, one can verify that Lemma 9.2 only blows up the universe size by a fixed polynomial (strictly speaking, the universe size does not change, but the instance size shrinks by a fixed polynomial factor). Hence, in the end we arrive at 3SUM instances whose universe size is still $n^{O(1)}$ (where the $O(1)$ depends on $\delta$ ). ∎

## 10 Reduction to Triangle Listing

In this section, we prove the following theorem.

#### Theorem 10.1.

Given a 3SUM instance on a size $n$ set $A\subset[n^{O(1)}]$ with additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)\leq n^{2+\delta}$ , a small parameter $\epsilon>0$ , and a parameter $P=n^{k\cdot\epsilon}\leq n$ for some integer $k$ , there is a deterministic reduction that reduces the 3SUM instance to $n^{o(1)}$ Triangle Listing instances on graphs with

- • $P^{2}\cdot n^{O(\epsilon)}$ nodes;

- • $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/P)$ maximum degree;

- • $n^{2+\delta+o(1)}/P+n^{4+o(1)}/P^{4}$ $4$ -cycles,

and we are required to report $n^{3+o(1)}/P^{2}$ triangles for each graph. Furthermore, the running time of the reduction is $O(n^{2-\epsilon}+n^{1+O(\epsilon)}\cdot P)$ .

### 10.1 Warm-up: randomized reduction

Before we prove Theorem 10.1, we first show a randomized version of the reduction and we later derandomize it. The reduction is similar to [ABF23]’s reduction from low-energy 3SUM to Triangle Listing with few $4$ -cycles (the difference is that they work over the group $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}$ for some prime $p$ and integer $d$ , while we work over integers), and also shares similar high-level structure with [JX23]’s reduction from strong 3SUM to Triangle Detection.

Let $p=\Theta(P)$ be a prime. Let $\mathcal{H}\colon\{-N,\ldots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , for $N=n^{O(1)}$ be the hash family constructed in Definition 5.5, which is almost linear “almost” almost $k$ -wise independent by Lemma 5.9. Note that in this case, two integers $x_{1}\neq x_{2}$ cannot have an $n^{o(1)}$ -relation, so the hash family is actually almost $2$ -wise independent.

Let $f,g,h$ be three hash functions sampled from $\mathcal{H}$ .

For any $a\neq b\in A$ , the probability $f(a)=f(b)$ is $O(1/p)$ . Therefore,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\left[\sum_{a,b\in A}[f(a)=f(b)]\right]=O(n^{2}/p). $$

Therefore, the number of $a\in A$ that is in the same hash bucket (under hash function $f$ ) with $\geq n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ numbers in $A$ is $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ . For these numbers, we can detect whether they are in any 3SUM solution in $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ total time, using the naive algorithm for 3SUM. Afterwards, we can remove these numbers from $A$ , so that all hash bucket (under hash function $f$ ) contains at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ numbers.

Similarly, after $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon})$ time pre-processing we can ensure that any number in $A$ is mapped to the same bucket with $\leq n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ other numbers under either $g$ or $h$ .

We will construct $n^{o(1)}$ graphs, one for every $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3})\in\Delta_{f}^{3}\times\Delta_{g}^{3}\times\Delta_{h}^{3}$ . The constructed graph will be a tripartite graph, where the nodes of the three parts are labeled by

$$ \{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\} $$

respectively. Next we describe the edges of the graph. We add an edge from a vertex $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ to $(x_{2},y_{2},z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if there is some $a\in A$ such that $x_{2}-x_{1}=f(a)+\delta_{f,1}$ , $y_{2}-y_{1}=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ and $z_{2}-z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,1}$ . Edges between other parts are similarly added, except that we replace $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{h,1})$ with $(\delta_{f,2},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{h,2})$ or $(\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,3})$ depending on which part it is. More precisely:

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ (the label is purely for convenience in the analysis, and does not technically appear in the Triangle Listing instances) between $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(x_{2},0,z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $x_{2}=f(a)+\delta_{f,1}$ , $-y_{1}=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ and $z_{2}-z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,1}$ .

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ between $(x_{2},0,z_{2})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(x_{3},y_{3},0)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{q}\times\{0\}$ if $x_{3}-x_{2}=f(a)+\delta_{f,2}$ , $y_{3}=g(a)+\delta_{g,2}$ and $-z_{2}=h(a)+\delta_{h,2}$ .

- • For any $a\in A$ , we add an edge with label $a$ between $(x_{3},y_{3},0)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}$ and $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $-x_{3}=f(a)+\delta_{f,3}$ , $y_{1}-y_{3}=g(a)+\delta_{g,3}$ and $z_{1}=h(a)+\delta_{h,3}$ .

We only keep one copy of all duplicated edges.

The construction of the graph is efficient. For instance, to find all edges between the first two parts, we enumerate $a\in A$ and $z\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , and then add edges between $(0,-g(a)-\delta_{g,1},z)\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and $(f(a)+\delta_{f,1},0,z+h(a)+\delta_{h,1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . The running time is essentially linear in the number of edges.

#### Number of Vertices.

Clearly, the number of vertices in the constructed graph is $O(p^{2})$ .

#### Maximum Degree.

Consider a vertex $(0,y,z)\in\{0\}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}$ in the first node part. In order for it to connect to some node in the second node part, there must exist some $a\in A$ where $-y=g(a)+\delta_{g,1}$ . By the pre-processing, the number of such $a$ is at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ . Similarly, in order for $(0,y,z)$ to connect to some node in the third node part, we need to have some $a\in A$ where $z=h(a)+\delta_{h,3}$ , so the number of such $a$ again is at most $n^{1+\epsilon}/p$ . Thus, the degree of $(0,y,z)$ is $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/p)$ . By symmetry, the maximum degree of the graph is $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/p)$ .

#### Number of Triangles.

First of all, if $a,b,c\in A$ have $a+b+c=0$ , then $f(a)+f(b)+f(c)\in f(a+b+c)-2\Delta_{f}\subseteq-3\Delta_{f}$ (note that as $f(0+0)-f(0)-f(0)\in\Delta_{f}$ , we must have $f(0)\in-\Delta_{f}$ ). Thus, there must exist $\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3}\in\Delta_{f}$ , so that $(f(a)+\delta_{f,1})+(f(b)+\delta_{f,2})+(f(c)+\delta_{f,3})=0$ . Similarly, must exist $\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3}\in\Delta_{g}$ , so that $(g(a)+\delta_{g,1})+(g(b)+\delta_{g,2})+(g(c)+\delta_{g,3})=0$ , and $\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3}\in\Delta_{h}$ , so that $(h(a)+\delta_{h,1})+(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})+(h(c)+\delta_{h,3})=0$ . Then the following three vertices must form a triangle in the graph constructed with parameters $(\delta_{f,1},\delta_{f,2},\delta_{f,3},\delta_{g,1},\delta_{g,2},\delta_{g,3},\delta_{h,1},\delta_{h,2},\delta_{h,3})$ :

$$ (0,-(g(a)+\delta_{g,1}),h(c)+\delta_{h,3}),\quad(f(a)+\delta_{f,1},0,-(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})),\quad(-(f(c)+\delta_{f,3}),g(b)+\delta_{g,2},0). $$

For any triangle in the constructed graph, it is not difficult to verify that the edge labels $a,b,c$ of the three edges of the triangle satisfy

$$ \begin{gathered}(f(a)+\delta_{f,1})+(f(b)+\delta_{f,2})+(f(c)+\delta_{f,3})=0,\\
(g(a)+\delta_{g,1})+(g(b)+\delta_{g,2})+(g(c)+\delta_{g,3})=0,\\
(h(a)+\delta_{h,1})+(h(b)+\delta_{h,2})+(h(c)+\delta_{h,3})=0.\end{gathered} $$

Thus, triples $(a,b,c)$ satisfying Eq. 25 are in one-to-one correspondence with triangles in the graph.

Eq. 25 implies that

$$ f(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{f}-3\Delta_{f},\quad g(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{g}-3\Delta_{g},\quad h(a+b+c)\in 2\Delta_{h}-3\Delta_{h}. $$

If $a+b+c\neq 0$ , then by Lemma 5.10, each of these equations holds with probability $n^{o(1)}/p$ , so the probability that they all hold is $n^{o(1)}/p^{3}$ . Furthermore, each triple $(a,b,c)$ can contribute at most $1$ triangle in each constructed graph. Thus, the expected number of triangles in each graph with edge labels $a,b,c$ for $a+b+c\neq 0$ is $n^{3+o(1)}/p^{3}$ , and it suffices to list more triangles than this number before we find an actual 3SUM solution if an actual 3SUM solution exists.

#### Number of Four-Cycles.

By symmetry, it suffices to consider the following two types of four-cycles:

- • The $4$ -cycle (with edge labels) is $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\overset{a_{1}}{-}(x_{2},0,z_{2})\overset{a_{2}}{-}(x_{3},y_{3},0)\overset{a_{3}}{-}(x_{4},0,z_{4})\overset{a_{4}}{-}(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ . Such a $4$ -cycle exists only if the following set of equations hold: $\displaystyle x_{2}\in f(a_{1})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{3}-x_{2}\in f(a_{2})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{3}-x_{4}\in f(a_{3})+\Delta_{f},\quad$ $\displaystyle x_{4}\in f(a_{4})+\Delta_{f},$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{1})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle y_{3}\in g(a_{2})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle y_{3}\in g(a_{3})+\Delta_{g},\quad$ $\displaystyle-y_{1}\in g(a_{4})+\Delta_{g},$ $\displaystyle z_{2}-z_{1}\in h(a_{1})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle-z_{2}\in h(a_{2})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle-z_{4}\in h(a_{3})+\Delta_{h},\quad$ $\displaystyle z_{4}-z_{1}\in h(a_{4})+\Delta_{h}.$ These equations imply

$$ \displaystyle f(a_{1})+f(a_{2})-f(a_{3})-f(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{f}-2\Delta_{f}, $$



$$ \displaystyle g(a_{1})-g(a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2})-g(a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g} $$



$$ \displaystyle h(a_{1})+h(a_{2})-h(a_{3})-h(a_{4})\in 2\Delta_{h}-2\Delta_{h}, $$

which further imply

$$ \begin{gathered}f(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{f}-4\Delta_{f},\\ g(a_{1}-a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2}-a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-2\Delta_{g}\\ h(a_{1}+a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4})\in 3\Delta_{h}-4\Delta_{h}.\end{gathered} $$

(26) Furthermore, each tuple $(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})$ satisfying Eq. 26 can contribute at most $n^{o(1)}$ such $4$ -cycles. Notice that if $a_{2}=a_{3}$ or $a_{1}=a_{4}$ , then the above walk from $(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ back to $(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ actually uses duplicated edges, so it is not a $4$ -cycle. - • The $4$ -cycle (with edge labels) is $(0,y_{1},z_{1})\overset{a_{1}}{-}(x_{2},0,z_{2})\overset{a_{2}}{-}(0,y_{3},z_{3})\overset{a_{3}}{-}(x_{4},0,z_{4})\overset{a_{4}}{-}(0,y_{1},z_{1})$ . $$ \displaystyle f(a_{1})-f(a_{2})\in\Delta_{f}-\Delta_{f},\quad f(a_{4})-f(a_{3})\in\Delta_{f}-\Delta_{f}, $$



$$ \displaystyle g(a_{1})-g(a_{4})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g},\quad g(a_{2})-g(a_{3})\in\Delta_{g}-\Delta_{g} $$

### 10.2 Derandomization

The randomness of the above construction comes from the random choices of the hash functions $f,g,h$ . By Definition 5.5, the size of the hash family is $p^{O(1)}$ , so it will be expensive to enumerate over all triples of hash functions when $p$ is big.
